meeting_header: Date: 2026-04-29 | Time: 15:00 - 15:52 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Sam Torres (BrightScale CTO), Maya Patel (BrightScale Eng Mgr), Rajiv Menon (BrightScale Infra)
summary: Redwood SE ran a throughput tuning deep dive focusing on continuous batching, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, token limits), KV cache sizing and quantization tradeoffs. BrightScale is evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted with on-prem VPC constraints; primary goals are steady 95th percentile latency under 120ms for short responses and cost target of < $0.002/token equivalent via batching and quantization. Agreed next steps: share config examples, export traces, and run a 4-week Dedicated pilot benchmark.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, quick intro — I'm Alex from Redwood, AE, and Priya is our SE.
[00:07] Priya: Hi, Sam, Maya, Rajiv, super excited to dig into throughput tuning today. We'll cover continuous batching behavior, scheduler knobs and practical knobs like max_num_seqs and token limits, and touch on KV cache and quantization.
[00:20] Sam: Thanks. Our main ask — we run a chat assistant, typical responses are 20-80 tokens, p95 latency target around 120ms, peak qps about 400, and we want to keep cost down. We also have strict VPC-only deployment for PII tenants.
[00:35] Maya: Also want to understand what changes we need on our side vs what Redwood does in the runtime.
[00:40] Priya: Great, we'll start with continuous batching basics. The runtime continuously groups incoming requests to amortize model kernel startup and fill CUDA kernels. Two knobs we often tune: max_num_seqs (max concurrent sequences per batch) and per-batch token cap (max_total_tokens).
[00:58] Priya: If you set max_num_seqs too high you'll increase throughput but may hurt tail latency for short requests because the scheduler waits to fill the batch. Conversely too low — you underutilize the GPU.
[01:15] Rajiv: How does the scheduler decide when to flush a partially-filled batch? Is it time-based or size-based?
[01:20] Priya: It's hybrid. We have a fill timer (default 8-12ms) and size thresholds. On Dedicated you can set the fill timer and the max hold time. For low-latency SLOs we recommend a small fill timer + dynamic padding.
[01:34] Sam: What about priority routing? Some of our tenants are high-priority and we can't add 10ms extra.
[01:39] Alex: You can tag requests with priority and we offer multi-queue scheduling: high-priority queue with aggressive flushing and smaller max_num_seqs. Lower priority jobs use larger batches to optimize cost.
[01:48] Maya: Can you explain max_num_seqs in practice? Example values?
[01:52] Priya: Sure — for 8x A100 class GPUs with a medium-sized Llama-variant, typical max_num_seqs we see in production is 8-32 depending on seq len. For BrightScale's short responses (20-80 tokens) start with max_num_seqs=12 and per-batch token cap at 2048 tokens then iterate.
[02:10] Rajiv: Is max_num_seqs per-AI-worker or per-GPU?
[02:14] Priya: Per inference worker process, which you can colocalize with GPU. The runtime shards KV-cache per worker.
[02:19] Sam: KV cache — we have prefix-heavy traffic, a lot of repeated prompts. How does Redwood's KV cache help?
[02:25] Priya: We do prefix caching: if the same prefix appears we reuse KV cache, which short-circuits repeated attention computation. Cache hit rate is key — we can suggest cache sizing and TTLs. Note sometimes the transcription in our internal docs says "KV cash" — sorry for the typo, it's KV cache.
[02:41] Maya: Any gotchas with cache invalidation for dynamic prompts?
[02:45] Priya: Yes — if prompts include timestamped or user-specific tokens you get low reuse. We recommend stable canonicalization of prompts and client-side prefix normalization. Also limit TTL so you don't bloat memory.
[02:59] Sam: About quantization — we want to squeeze cost, how aggressive can we be?
[03:04] Priya: For inference, 4-bit quant can yield substantial throughput gains but watch quality regressions. Our recommendation: run a short eval suite on 4-bit and 8-bit int8/4bit mixes. For many retrieval-augmented workflows 4-bit is fine; for instruction-following you may prefer int8. We can provide quant profiles per model.
[03:23] Rajiv: Do quantized models affect KV cache layout or token latency?
[03:27] Priya: Not materially for KV layout, but kernel execution time improves. The runtime picks kernels optimized for the quant format which can reduce per-token time significantly.
[03:35] [00:03:40] Speaker 1: Hmm, question on token limits — do you cap tokens per request?
[03:41] Priya: We recommend a per-request max_tokens and a per-batch token cap. The latter prevents one large request from delaying many small ones. For example set per-request max 512 and per-batch cap 2048.
[03:52] Sam: If a single request would exceed the per-batch cap do you split it?
[03:55] Priya: Yes, we stream and chunk long generations; long contexts can be handled by chunking and stitching. That said chunking impacts latency and complexity.
[04:05] Maya: Can you show us a scheduler config example?
[04:08] Priya: (shares link in chat) — example: {fill_ms: 10, max_num_seqs: 12, max_total_tokens: 2048, priority_queues: ["high","normal","low"], flush_on_priority: true}. We'll send the exact YAML after the call.
[04:26] Rajiv: On VPC/on-prem: our security team needs to know what changes when we move to Private. Is there any scheduler difference?
[04:33] Alex: Functionally the scheduler is the same; differences are in network topology, metrics collection endpoints, and where logs land. For on-prem we run the same runtime but with customer-managed KMS and audit logs.
[04:45] Priya: One nuance: when you run on-prem with smaller pool sizes you need tighter tuning — smaller pool means less opportunity to form big batches, so you lean more on quantization and efficient kernels.
[04:58] Sam: For Dedicated vs Hosted — is there automatic fallback to hosted if Dedicated capacity is saturated?
[05:03] Alex: Yes, you can enable routing fallbacks. We can configure policy: prefer Dedicated, fall back to hosted-compatible model variant or lower-cost batch profile. That's part of the rollout policy.
[05:15] Maya: We have a hard requirement for audit logs and retention in EU. Can Dedicated/Private meet that?
[05:21] Alex: Yes — Private supports region-local logging and configurable retention; Dedicated has enterprise SLAs and can be configured to comply. We'll include our SOC2/ISO artifacts.
[05:31] Priya: Back to throughput tuning — some practical experiments to run: 1) baseline with one worker, max_num_seqs low (4) to see latencies, 2) bump to 12 and measure p95 and token throughput, 3) enable 4-bit quant and compare quality/throughput. Also capture kernel occupancy and GPU SM utilization.
[05:51] Rajiv: What metrics should we export?
[05:54] Priya: Per-request latency histogram, batch size distribution, batch fill time, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, and memory high-water marks.
[06:07] Sam: Can Redwood run the initial benchmark or do we need to run it?
[06:10] Alex: We can run a pilot on Dedicated for you — typical 2-4 week benchmark. We'll handle setup and initial tuning with your traces.
[06:20] Maya: Are there known pitfalls with max_num_seqs and request priority mixing?
[06:24] Priya: Yes — if you set a global max_num_seqs high but also have strict low latency for premium customers, ensure you use per-queue overrides; otherwise premium requests will sit behind batch filling.
[06:36] [00:06:40] Speaker 2: Quick question — does Redwood support dynamic batching per-model?
[06:40] Priya: Yes, per-model and per-route configs. You can have a small, fast model for short responses and a larger one for high-quality long responses, then route requests by intent.
[06:49] Rajiv: Anything else about token limits that trips teams up?
[06:52] Priya: Teams often forget to limit client-side the user input length — a single user can send huge context which then monopolizes resources. We suggest server-side hard caps and client-side validation.
[07:02] Sam: Do you have any ready-made dashboards for these metrics?
[07:06] Alex: Redwood Console has per-route latency/token breakdown, batch histograms, and tracing hooks — we can give you dashboard templates.
[07:15] Maya: For the KV cache TTLs what's a typical default?
[07:18] Priya: Defaults around 30 minutes for repeated prefixes, but this depends heavily on reuse patterns. We'll recommend TTL based on your traces.
[07:27] Rajiv: On the topic of quantization again, how do we validate quality automatically?
[07:31] Priya: We recommend a prompt set that represents your user distribution and run A/B evals with automated metrics plus human spot checks. Redwood Optimize can automate regression alerts on your eval set.
[07:44] Sam: About batching and token caps — any math we can use? Like expected latency = fill_time + compute_time_per_token * tokens / batch_size?
[07:52] Priya: Roughly yes. Fill_time depends on qps and fill_ms; compute_time scales with tokens*batch_multiplier. We can provide a model-specific provider profile that estimates per-token compute.
[08:03] Maya: Can you share an example config that gave you 3x throughput improvements?
[08:07] Priya: Yes — for one customer we increased max_num_seqs from 6 to 18, added int8 kernels, and tuned fill_ms from 20ms to 8ms, plus prefix caching — net 2.8x throughput and p95 still within SLO. We'll include that case study.
[08:23] [00:08:30] Speaker 1: I'm seeing occasional "KV cash thrash" in our logs, any guidance?
[08:28] Priya: Kv cash thrash — likely typo in logs but real issue is cache eviction storms when TTLs align. Stagger TTLs and use LRU with warmed prefills for common prefixes.
[08:40] Sam: For our pilot — if we send traces how soon can you start tuning?
[08:44] Alex: Once we have traces and a small config, Priya's team can start within 3 business days.
[08:49] Priya: We'll need per-request timestamps and token counts. If you can export one evening of peak and one off-peak that's ideal.
[08:59] Maya: Any quick wins we can do on our side now?
[09:02] Priya: Canonicalize prompts, enforce client max input length, enable prefix caching for stable prompts, and try int8 first on a small eval set.
[09:12] Sam: Let's summarize next steps.
[09:14] Alex: Recap: 1) Priya sends scheduler knob docs and YAML example (due 2026-05-03), 2) BrightScale exports traces (due 2026-05-06), 3) Alex sends pilot SOW and pricing (due 2026-05-05), 4) Run a 2-4 week Dedicated pilot to benchmark throughput with quantization.
[09:33] Maya: Sounds good. We'll get traces and sync with security on Private deployment docs.
[09:38] Priya: I'll also include a checklist for metrics and dashboards to capture.
[09:43] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links.
[09:48] Sam: Thanks all.
[09:50] [END]
